patterns.name: Character Frequency Counter
patterns.explanation: Maintain a count of each character (array of size 26 for lowercase ASCII, or a hash map for Unicode). Compare two strings by comparing their counters; detect anagrams, isomorphism, and frequency-bounded substrings.
patterns.when_to_use: Anagrams, permutations, 'is one a permutation of the other', isomorphic strings, finding all anagrams in a string (paired with sliding window).
patterns.intuition: Character set is small. A string of length N over alphabet σ has a frequency vector in ℕ^σ. Equality of frequency vectors == anagram. Two strings are isomorphic iff their character→character maps are bijective.
common_pitfalls: Using a hash map when an `int[26]` would do, paying constant-factor overhead
Forgetting to clear the counter between iterations
Treating uppercase and lowercase as the same when the problem says they differ
Using `==` on counter arrays in languages without value-equality

patterns.name: Palindrome Expansion
patterns.explanation: For each center (each character and each gap between characters), expand outward while the two sides match. Finds all palindromic substrings in O(N²).
patterns.when_to_use: Longest palindromic substring, count palindromic substrings, palindrome partitioning. The center-expansion idea is the natural and simplest O(N²) approach.
patterns.intuition: Every palindrome has a center: either a character (odd length) or a gap (even length). 2N−1 centers; each expansion costs O(N) in the worst case.
common_pitfalls: Handling only odd-length palindromes and missing all even-length ones
Returning length instead of substring or vice versa
Using DP where center expansion is simpler
Off-by-one in expansion bounds

patterns.name: KMP & Failure Function
patterns.explanation: Knuth–Morris–Pratt builds a 'failure function' (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, for each prefix of the pattern) and uses it to skip rechecking matched characters. Substring search in O(N + M).
patterns.when_to_use: Substring search; longest happy prefix; finding the smallest repeating unit of a string ('repeated substring pattern'). Whenever you see 'find pattern in text' and constraints rule out O(N·M).
patterns.intuition: After a partial match of length k that fails, you don't restart from scratch — the failure function tells you the longest already-matched suffix that is also a prefix, so you continue from there.
common_pitfalls: Off-by-one in the failure function (it's defined on prefixes, not on indices directly)
Resetting the matched length naively to 0 instead of using `lps[matched-1]`
Confusing KMP with Z-function
Implementing without a clear definition and getting subtle bugs

patterns.name: Z-Algorithm
patterns.explanation: Compute, for each index i, the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. Single linear scan with a 'Z-box' window.
patterns.when_to_use: Pattern matching (concatenate `pattern + sentinel + text` and look for Z-values equal to pattern length); period detection; lexicographic comparisons of suffixes.
patterns.intuition: Maintain the rightmost Z-box `[l, r]` seen so far. For index i ≤ r, you can copy a Z-value from earlier and only extend if necessary. Amortized linear.
common_pitfalls: Building Z over `pattern$text` but forgetting the sentinel and getting cross-matches
Returning the Z-array but not knowing how to read 'pattern occurs at position i'
Confusing Z-values (suffix matches against prefix) with KMP failures (prefix–suffix overlap)
Implementing in O(N²) by mistake

patterns.name: Rolling Hash (Rabin–Karp)
patterns.explanation: Hash a string treating its characters as digits in some base (typically 31 or 131) modulo a large prime. Sliding the window updates the hash in O(1).
patterns.when_to_use: Substring search with multiple patterns; longest duplicate substring; equality testing of many ranges (combine with prefix hashes); plagiarism-style detection.
patterns.intuition: Polynomial hashing turns string equality into integer equality. Rolling means you can roll the window in O(1). Use double hashing (two hash pairs) to reduce collision probability to ~1/p² for cryptographically uneventful inputs.
common_pitfalls: Using a single weak modulus and getting hash collisions on adversarial inputs
Negative numbers under `%` (use `((x % M) + M) % M`)
Not precomputing `base^k mod M` and recomputing it inside the loop
Forgetting to verify a hash hit with an actual character comparison
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N + M) expected, O(N·M) worst case with bad hash

patterns.name: Manacher's Algorithm
patterns.explanation: Compute the longest palindromic substring centered at every position in O(N) using a clever mirror-and-extend strategy with the rightmost palindrome boundary.
patterns.when_to_use: When O(N²) palindrome expansion is too slow (N ≈ 10^6), or when you need the full palindrome-radius array as a building block for further analysis.
patterns.intuition: Inside the rightmost-known palindrome, the radius at i mirrors the radius at the symmetric index — bounded by the right edge. Extend only when you go past the edge.
common_pitfalls: Not transforming the string with sentinels (`#a#b#c#`) to unify odd and even cases
Off-by-one when reading back the original substring from the transformed array
Forgetting that the mirror radius is *capped* by `r - i`
Implementing it from memory without verifying on simple cases
